Maladaptive Strategies.value: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy
Talking with others about the event or its aftermath
Being reminded of the event by others

Threat.value: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

Negative Appraisals.value: The world is a dangerous place
I have to be on guard all the time
I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: The appraisal of permanent bodily damage is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile and trauma context. The other selected items consistently reflect ongoing external danger and hyperarousal (world dangerous, on guard, startle, false alarms, threat in silence) plus intrusive sensory memory, but there are no corroborating memory, threat, or strategy items indicating injury-focused trauma consequences, pain, disability, or body-related threat. For a refugee trauma profile, this isolated somatic-damage belief is not impossible, but in this item set it stands out as clinically incoherent with the dominant formulation of danger-based threat and avoidance.

vignette: Elias was nineteen when the shelling began in his hometown. He had been ushered into the stone-walled cellar beneath his family's apartment, the heavy iron door sealing them into damp darkness. For hours, there was only the muffled thud of distant impacts, a silence so absolute it pressed against his eardrums. Then the ground shuddered, glass shattered upstairs, and boots pounded on the stairs. He folded himself onto the concrete floor, knees drawn to his chest, shoulders hunched against the cold stone, breathing in shallow, controlled pulls until the footsteps passed. He survived because he stayed quiet, stayed low, and stayed alert. What he knew then was that safety was an illusion and danger arrived without warning. After relocating to the United States as a refugee, he navigated resettlement services and eventually entered an accelerated legal training program, now working as a Public Defender in a state office. The cellar did not leave him. His mind never stopped scanning. He came to believe the world was a dangerous place, that he had to be on guard all the time, especially careful because you never knew what could happen next. In his daily work, every ring, echo, and sudden door slam demanded a response. An unusual silence in a room would tighten his chest immediately; he was certain something dangerous was about to happen. When a stapler clicked in his office or a car backfired on the street, his shoulders would jerk, his breath would catch, and his pulse would race as if the iron door were closing again. He would often find himself stepping back from a doorway, reacting as if he were in danger even when nothing was actually wrong. The past did not visit him as a narrative. It arrived as photographs: the grain of the cellar floor, the rusted hinge, the sliver of light that had cut through the crack beneath it. When those images surfaced, his body mirrored the old posture instantly, knees tight, spine curved, muscles locked in the same cramped alignment he had held for hours. Other times, the terror would wash over him without any clear picture, just the raw, unfiltered weight of the fear he had felt that night. Beside these reactions, Elias began watching his own mind with relentless precision. He monitored his thoughts constantly, searching for any sign that he was going crazy, counting his words, noting his breath, checking his focus like a man inspecting a structural beam for hairline fractures. He would not talk with others about the event or its aftermath, deflecting gentle questions about his past or changing the subject when colleagues mentioned the conflicts in his former country. Being reminded of the event by others was something he avoided carefully, steering conversations toward procedural deadlines or courtroom logistics instead. His work placed him inside the very environment where his sensitivities surfaced most sharply. During court recesses, Elias would sit in the unused overflow room; the absence of sound would tighten his chest, and he was certain something dangerous was about to happen. He mapped his caseload around predictable rhythms, turning down last-minute client meetings that required him to sit in closed offices where he could not monitor the entrance. His partner, Mara, had noticed how he pulled back. When she asked if he wanted to talk about what was weighing on him, he would shake his head and say he was just tired, then retreat to the other side of the living room to review case files. He had come to believe that staying close to the evidence was safer than leaning into uncertainty, but the distance between them grew with every avoided conversation. At twenty-one, Elias walked into a community mental health clinic because the volume of his own reactions had begun to interfere with his ability to function. He had missed two critical filing deadlines after becoming so fixated on a sudden noise outside his office window that he lost the thread of his afternoon. What frightened him most was not the memories themselves, but the way his body obeyed them before his mind could catch up, and the fear that he was fracturing under the weight of it all. He sat in the intake room with his hands folded tightly in his lap, hoping to find a way to lower the volume on the alarms he could not turn off, and wondering if anyone could help him stop waiting for the next blow.
